title: Real or Racket

source.quote: racket feelings never help finish the situation.

setting: Two weeks after the release mess. Thursday, 4:50pm, sprint retro wrapping up. Arjun has been quiet the whole meeting, then speaks up as people start closing their laptops.

L1.line: Ha, whatever, it doesn't matter. I'll just fix it again, like always.
cues: doesn't name what's wrong or ask anyone for anything
L1.question: Is Arjun expressing an authentic feeling here, or a racket feeling?

options.text: Authentic frustration - he was genuinely overworked, so saying it plainly will get it fixed.
options.feedback: He isn't naming anything specific or asking for a change - he's not saying what's wrong, just replaying a line. That's not what authentic, problem-solving frustration sounds like.

options.text: A racket feeling - it feels real to him, but the bitter laugh and "like always" are signals of an old script belief being replayed, and saying it changes nothing.
options.feedback: Right. The tell isn't whether it's genuine - he's really feeling it. The tell is that expressing it doesn't move anything, and the recycled line is the signature of a racket, not fresh anger about today.

options.text: A racket feeling, simply because he's being negative - any complaint like this is a racket.
options.feedback: Close, but not for that reason. Negativity alone isn't the tell - authentic anger can sound sharp too. The tell here is specifically that it never resolves anything, not that it sounds bad.

L1.lesson: A racket feeling can feel completely real - the tell isn't whether it's genuine, it's whether expressing it ever finishes anything. Arjun's bitter laugh and his recycled line ("like always") are signals of a discount, not fresh, present-tense anger about today.

L2.intro: You want to find out if there's a real, solvable problem here - not just hand him another stroke for the old story. What do you say?

beats.line: Ha, whatever, it doesn't matter. I'll just fix it again, like always.

options.text: You always do end up fixing it, don't you.
options.outcome: Arjun gives a small, satisfied nod. "Yeah. Story of my life." The meeting moves on; nothing about the workload changes.
options.lesson: Agreeing with the racket line pays him a stamp for it - this is Fanita English's racketeering: trading strokes for the feeling instead of looking at the actual problem underneath it.

options.text: That sounds exhausting. Take it easy today.
options.outcome: He softens. "Thanks... I guess." He's comforted, but the actual workload problem stays exactly as it was.
options.lesson: Kind, but it strokes the racket feeling rather than the unmet need underneath it - useful once, but it won't move the real problem forward.

options.text: What specifically needs fixing, and whose is it to fix?
options.outcome: Arjun blinks, the laugh dropping. "Actually... the deploy script is still broken from last sprint. I keep patching it by hand instead of flagging it." Now there's something to solve.
options.lesson: An Adult question toward the actual problem doesn't feed the racket feeling - it surfaces the real, solvable issue the racket was substituting for.

options.text: Must be rough feeling like it's always on you.
options.outcome: Arjun shrugs, not quite landing on it. "I don't know, maybe."
options.lesson: Naming an authentic feeling (mad, sad, scared, glad) can help - but guessing at it from outside, without evidence, risks landing as just another stroke for the Child rather than a real opening.

fields.label: If Priya had said "That sounds exhausting, take it easy today" instead, write in under 50 words what would have happened to the deploy script problem - and whether Arjun's racket feeling would still be sitting there next retro.

Arjun's tone barely changes between the racket line and the deploy script admission. In under 60 words, explain what actually marks the second one as authentic rather than racket, since the bitterness is still there.

echo.setting: A week later: Arjun says the same kind of line about a different ticket.
echo.line: Ha, whatever, I'll just handle it, like always.
echo.shape: same three-option diagnose shape as L1
